info.title: MoltSets API
info.description: MoltSets is an identity resolution API. Use it to resolve emails, LinkedIn profiles, and IP addresses into enriched contact and company data, including business and personal emails, mobile phone numbers, and firmographic details.

bearerAuth.description: Pass your API key as a Bearer token. Keys follow the format `ms_XXXXXXXXXXX`.

UserAgentHeader.name: User-Agent
UserAgentHeader.description: Identifies the calling client. Any non-empty value is accepted — MoltSets does not validate its contents. Requests without this header are rejected with `403 Forbidden` (`error.code`: `forbidden`).

fair_use.description: Fair Use Policy headroom for the record limits that apply to this call.

records_remaining_5h.description: Records you can still request in the current rolling 5-hour window.

records_reset_5h.description: ISO 8601 timestamp when the 5-hour records window resets.

records_remaining_1w.description: Records you can still request in the current rolling 1-week window.

records_reset_1w.description: ISO 8601 timestamp when the 1-week records window resets.

tokens_used.description: Tokens consumed by this call. `0` on a `not_found`. Present on token-bound (free) accounts only — accounts on an unlimited subscription omit it.

tokens_remaining.description: Token balance after this call. Present on token-bound (free) accounts only.

personal_email_restricted.description: Present and `true` only when the call actually withheld personal-email data because the account does not have the personal-email surface. Read a missing personal email as a plan boundary, not as absent data.

identity_hashes_restricted.description: Present and `true` only when the call stripped `business_email_sha256s` because the account is on the \$397 or \$997 plan. Read a missing SHA256 hash as a plan boundary, not as absent data.

retry_after.description: Seconds until the binding Fair Use window unlocks. Present on Fair Use 429s, and on a batch that returned partial results because items were dropped for Fair Use — the same value is sent as a `Retry-After` header.

phone_tokens_used.description: Phone tokens consumed by this call. `linkedin_to_mobile_phone` only; `0` on a `not_found`.

phone_tokens_remaining.description: Phone tokens remaining after this call. `linkedin_to_mobile_phone` only.

Metadata.description: Per-call metadata. `fair_use` is always present on a tool call; the remaining fields appear only where they apply.

ErrorInvalidInput.description: The request body is malformed, or a parameter is missing, malformed, or outside its allowed values.

message.example: Message describing the nature of the invalid input.

ErrorUnauthorized.description: The API key or OAuth token is missing, invalid, or revoked.

ErrorInternal.description: Returned when the call could not complete — usually because the endpoint is unavailable, though an oversized request can also cause it. Retry with a smaller request first. Never charged.

ErrorPlanRestricted.description: The request is refused. `forbidden` means the request has no `User-Agent` header — add one (any non-empty value). `plan_restricted` means the tool is not part of the account's plan — today, the dedicated personal-email tools on a plan without the personal-email surface, and the ad-audience tools (`email_to_maid`, `business_email_to_sha256`, `linkedin_to_sha256`) on the \$397 and \$997 plans. It is a plan condition, so there is no `Retry-After` and topping up tokens does not clear it. `account_inactive` means the account itself is not active — log in and subscribe to a plan.

message.example: Personal email lookups are not available on your plan. Contact support@moltsets.com to request access.

ErrorNotFound.description: Returned only when the tool name in the URL does not exist or has been retired. A lookup that finds no data is **not** a 404 — it returns HTTP 200 with `status: "not_found"`.

ErrorRateLimit.description: Rate or Fair Use limit. `rate_limited` is the burst/IP guard; `fair_use_limit_exceeded` means a Fair Use **record** window is exhausted (or, on the free tier, the one-time search trial); `fair_use_requests_exceeded` means the 5-hour **request** window is exhausted; `search_concurrency_exceeded` means too many `search_people` / `search_companies` calls are running at the same time for the plan (Free and $27: 3, $97: 5, $397 and $997: 8). The Fair Use codes carry `metadata.retry_after` and a `Retry-After` header. `search_concurrency_exceeded` carries `Retry-After: 1` — retry after 1 second and run fewer searches in parallel.

message.example: Fair use record limit reached. Retry after the window resets.

retry_after.description: Seconds until the binding window unlocks. Also sent as a `Retry-After` header. Absent when the limit is a plan condition rather than a window (free-tier search trial exhausted).

ErrorInsufficientTokens.description: Out of credit. `insufficient_tokens` means the token balance cannot cover the call; `insufficient_phone_tokens` means the phone token balance (from the separate phone token subscription) cannot cover a mobile-phone result. On a batch, unaffordable items are dropped and the response returns partial results with this error block rather than failing the whole call.

ErrorForbidden.description: The request has no `User-Agent` header. Add one — any non-empty value is accepted.

post.description: The People Search API lets you search MoltSets' contact database for people by name, job title, company, industry, country, seniority, or department. Use `title` for the job title or role — it matches the title field alone, so it is far more precise than putting a role in `query`. Use `query` for the person's name, or for loose natural-language phrases when you have nothing more specific. To find people at a specific company, use `company` (company name) or `company_domain` (website domain) rather than putting the employer in `query`. Use the exact filters (`country`, `state`, `city`, `seniority`, `industry`, `department` or `functional_area`, `employee_range`, `revenue_range`) to narrow further — `employee_range` and `revenue_range` scope to people at companies of that size or revenue without needing a specific company. Combining `query` with filters gives the most precise matches. Every result comes back ranked, with a higher `_score` meaning a stronger match. Every positive filter accepts either a single value or a list of values. A list is OR within its field and AND across fields, so `title: ["CEO", "CMO"]` with `country: ["United States", "Canada"]` means (CEO or CMO) in (United States or Canada) — one search instead of one per value, with every match ranked together. The `exclude_*` parameters (`exclude_company_domain`, `exclude_country`, `exclude_state`, `exclude_industry`, `exclude_seniority`, `exclude_employee_range`) work the other way round: each one also takes a list, but removes matches rather than selecting them. `exclude_company_domain` is how you suppress companies you already have. Exclusions narrow a search but cannot be the whole search — you still need at least one positive input. **Use this endpoint to:** - Build targeted lead lists for outbound sales - Identify decision makers at specific target accounts - Populate outbound sequences with verified contact data **Fair Use Policy:** This API is subject to our Fair Use Policy for Search. **Outcomes:** A lookup that finds nothing is not an error. It returns HTTP `200` with `status: "not_found"`, empty or null `results`, and the usual `metadata` — and costs no tokens, though it still counts as one request against your Fair Use requests limit. Read `status`, not the HTTP code, to tell a hit from a miss. The API's only `404` is an unknown or retired tool name.

query.description: Full-text search across full_name, first_name, last_name, company name, title (~85% filled), and headline (~65% filled) using cross-field matching. Multi-word queries distribute terms across fields — "John Smith" matches first_name: John AND last_name: Smith rather than requiring either field alone to contain the full string. Best for person names, and for loose natural-language phrases when nothing more specific fits. For a job title or role, use the `title` filter instead: a role placed here is diluted across names and company names and only needs most of its terms to match, so "Account Executive" in `query` can also return Account Managers. Likewise use `seniority` for level (VP, Director, C-suite), and `company` or `company_domain` for a specific employer. Categorical values like country or seniority belong in their own filter params rather than this field.

title.description: Job title filter (~85% filled) — scopes results to people whose job title matches, and the precise way to search by role. The match is analysed rather than literal: a one or two word title requires every word, so "Account Executive" will not return Account Managers. A longer title requires 75% of its words, rounded down — a three or four word title must match all but one, a five or six word title all but two. That allowance is what stops function words breaking a match, so "VP of Sales" still finds "VP, Sales". Extra words in the stored title are always fine: "Account Executive" matches "Senior Account Executive, SMB". Prefer this over putting a role in `query`. For seniority level use the `seniority` filter, which is a clean enumerated list, and use `title` for the role or function itself — the two combine, e.g. `title: "Sales"` with `seniority: "VP"`. Around 15% of profiles carry no title at all, and those can never match a title filter. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `title: ["CEO", "CMO"]` returns records matching either.

company.description: Company name filter — scopes results to people whose employer's name matches. Analysed match: every word you provide must appear in the company name, so extra words in the stored name are fine ("Acme" matches "Acme Corporation"). Use this when you have a company name but not its domain; if you have the domain, prefer `company_domain`, which is more precise. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `company: ["Acme", "Globex"]` returns records matching either.

company_domain.description: Company domain filter — scopes results to people at the company with this website domain. Full URLs are normalised automatically ("https://www.acme.com/about" → "acme.com"), so there is no need to strip the protocol or path yourself. The most precise way to target a single company — prefer it over `company` whenever you know the domain. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `company_domain: ["acme.com", "stripe.com"]` returns records matching either. A list can hold up to 100 domains.

country.description: Exact country name filter (~99% filled — most reliable filter). Must match the stored value exactly. Top values by volume: "United States", "India", "United Kingdom", "Brazil", "Canada", "France", "Mexico", "Australia", "China", "Spain", "Netherlands", "Italy", "Indonesia", "Germany", "Philippines", "Turkey", "South Africa", "Saudi Arabia", "Argentina", "Singapore", "United Arab Emirates", "Colombia", "South Korea", "Malaysia", "Poland", "Belgium", "Switzerland", "Ireland", "Sweden", "Denmark", "Norway", "Austria", "Portugal", "Israel", "New Zealand", "Finland", "Greece", "Hungary", "Romania", "Ukraine". Use the full English country name. "UK" and "HK" also exist in the data as dirty values — prefer "United Kingdom" and "Hong Kong". Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `country: ["United States", "Canada"]` returns records matching either.

state.description: Exact state or region name filter on the person's location. Accepts the full name with standard capitalisation or its abbreviation — "Texas" and "TX" both work. Canadian provinces match by their two-letter code too — "Ontario" or "ON", "British Columbia" or "BC", "Quebec" or "QC". Combine with `country` for precision. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `state: ["Texas", "Florida"]` returns records matching either.

city.description: Exact city name filter on the person's location. Must match the stored value exactly, with standard capitalisation. City names repeat across regions, so combine with `state` and/or `country` to disambiguate — e.g. city: "Portland", state: "Oregon". Matches only the exact stored city, not its suburbs — for a metro-area search prefer `state` or `country`. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `city: ["Austin", "Dallas"]` returns records matching either.

seniority.description: Exact seniority level filter (~60% filled). Must match one of the enumerated values exactly, including the space in "C Suite" (not a hyphen). Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `seniority: ["VP", "C Suite"]` returns records matching either.

industry.description: Exact current industry filter (~60% filled). These 22 buckets are the only supported values, and must match exactly, including capitalisation and punctuation (e.g. the ampersand in "Marketing & Advertising"). Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `industry: ["Information Technology", "Finance and Banking"]` returns records matching either.

department.description: Exact department filter (~60% filled). Shares its underlying data with `functional_area` — use one or the other, not both. Must match one of the enumerated values exactly, including capitalisation and punctuation (e.g. the ampersand in "Medical & Health"). Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `department: ["Sales", "Marketing"]` returns records matching either.

functional_area.description: Exact functional area filter (~60% filled). Shares its underlying data with `department` — use one or the other, not both. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `functional_area: ["Sales", "Marketing"]` returns records matching either.

employee_range.description: Exact employee-count range filter on the person's current employer — finds people at companies of a certain size without needing to name a specific company. These eight numeric bands are the only supported values, and use the same vocabulary as `search_companies`. Combine with other filters, e.g. `seniority: "VP"`, `employee_range: "51-200"`. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `employee_range: ["51-200", "201-500"]` returns records matching either.

revenue_range.description: Exact annual revenue range filter on the person's current employer — finds people at companies of a certain revenue without needing to name a specific company. These seven bands are the only supported values, and use the same vocabulary as `search_companies`. "Above $50M" is a flat catch-all for all revenue over $50M; there is no finer band above it. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `revenue_range: ["$10M - $20M", "$20M - $50M"]` returns records matching either.

naics_code.description: Exact NAICS industry code filter on the person's current employer (~50% filled). Works at any level of the hierarchy, from the 2-digit sector ("23" = Construction, "54" = Professional Services) through to the 6-digit national industry ("541120" = Offices of Notaries, "511210" = Software Publishers). Use a short code for broad industry targeting and a longer code for precision. The most standardised industry filter available — prefer it over `industry` when you need fine-grained targeting. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `naics_code: ["5112", "5415"]` returns records matching either.

linkedin_industry.description: Exact LinkedIn industry label filter on the person's current employer. Uses LinkedIn's own industry vocabulary, which is far finer-grained than the 22 buckets in `industry`. Must match the stored label exactly, with standard capitalisation — for example "Software Development", "Hospitality", "Legal Services", "Wellness and Fitness Services", "Construction", "Staffing and Recruiting". Use when a niche industry cannot be expressed by the broad `industry` buckets. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `linkedin_industry: ["Software Development", "IT Services and IT Consulting"]` returns records matching either.

exclude_company_domain.description: Company domains to exclude. People at any listed company are dropped from the results — this is the suppression list, so pass the accounts you already have (existing customers, current vendors, your own company) and they never come back. Full URLs are normalised automatically, exactly as with `company_domain`. Excluded records cost you nothing: they consume no tokens and no fair use records, so excluding here is always cheaper than filtering the results yourself. A list can hold up to 100 domains.

exclude_country.description: Countries to exclude. People in any listed country are dropped. Accepts the same values as `country` — use it when you want everywhere except a few places.

exclude_state.description: States or regions to exclude. People in any listed state are dropped. Accepts the same values as `state` (full names or abbreviations). Combine with a positive `country` — for example `country: "United States"` with `exclude_state: ["California"]`.

exclude_industry.description: Industries to exclude. People whose current industry is any listed value are dropped. Accepts the same values as `industry`. Around 40% of profiles carry no industry at all, and exclusion only removes profiles that positively carry a listed value — so those profiles still appear.

exclude_seniority.description: Seniority levels to exclude. People at any listed level are dropped. Accepts the same values as `seniority` (note the space in "C Suite"). Same caveat as `exclude_industry`: profiles with no seniority on record are not excluded.

exclude_employee_range.description: Employer size bands to exclude. People at companies in any listed band are dropped. Accepts the same values as `employee_range` — for example ["1-10", "11-20"] to skip very small companies, or ["5001+"] to skip enterprises.

limit.description: Number of results to return (default: 10, max: 25).

offset.description: Number of results to skip for pagination (default: 0). Use with limit to page through results — e.g. offset: 10 to get the second page of 10 results.

Use `query` for free text company name search, `domain` for an exact lookup by website domain, and the filters (`industry`, `employee_range`, `revenue_range`) to narrow your results. Combining `query` with filters gives the most precise matches. Every result comes back ranked, with a higher `_score` meaning a stronger match. A list is OR within its field and AND across fields, so `industry: ["Information Technology", "Finance and Banking"]` with `country: ["United States", "Canada"]` means (Information Technology or Finance and Banking) in (United States or Canada) — one search instead of one per value, with every match ranked together. The `exclude_*` parameters (`exclude_domain`, `exclude_industry`, `exclude_employee_range`, `exclude_revenue_range`) work the other way round: each one also takes a list, but removes matches rather than selecting them. `exclude_domain` is how you suppress accounts you already have. Exclusions narrow a search but cannot be the whole search — you still need at least one positive input. **Use this endpoint to:** - Build prospect lists for account-based marketing - Qualify target accounts before outreach - Enrich CRM records with firmographic data **Fair Use Policy:** This API is subject to our Fair Use Policy for Search. **Outcomes:** A lookup that finds nothing is not an error. It returns HTTP `200` with `status: "not_found"`, empty or null `results`, and the usual `metadata` — and costs no tokens, though it still counts as one request against your Fair Use requests limit. Read `status`, not the HTTP code, to tell a hit from a miss. The API's only `404` is an unknown or retired tool name.

query.description: Full-text search across company name only. Do not put domain, industry, employee size, or revenue here — use the dedicated filter params for those.

domain.description: Exact company domain filter. Full URLs are normalised automatically ("https://www.acme.com/about" → "acme.com"), so there is no need to strip the protocol or path yourself. Prefer this over `query` when you know the domain, since it is a precise match rather than a text search. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `domain: ["acme.com", "stripe.com"]` returns records matching either.

industry.description: Exact industry filter. These 22 buckets are the only supported values, and must match exactly, including capitalisation and punctuation (note the ampersand in "Marketing & Advertising"). For a niche the buckets cannot express — insurance carriers, aerospace, mining — use `linkedin_industry` instead. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `industry: ["Information Technology", "Finance and Banking"]` returns records matching either.

employee_range.description: Exact employee count range filter. These eight numeric bands are the only supported values — "1-10" holds the most records by a wide margin, "5001+" the fewest. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `employee_range: ["51-200", "201-500"]` returns records matching either.

revenue_range.description: Exact annual revenue range filter. These seven bands are the only supported values — "$500k - $1M" is the most common. "Above $50M" is a flat catch-all for all revenue over $50M; there is no finer band above it, so use it for any large-enterprise revenue target. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `revenue_range: ["$10M - $20M", "$20M - $50M"]` returns records matching either.

naics_code.description: Exact NAICS industry code filter (~50% filled). Works at any level of the hierarchy, from the 2-digit sector ("23" = Construction, "54" = Professional Services) through to the 6-digit national industry ("541120" = Offices of Notaries, "511210" = Software Publishers). Use a short code for broad industry targeting and a longer code for precision — the most standardised industry filter available. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `naics_code: ["5112", "5415"]` returns records matching either.

linkedin_industry.description: Exact LinkedIn industry label filter (~85% filled). Uses LinkedIn's own industry vocabulary, which is far finer-grained than the 22 buckets in `industry`. Must match the stored label exactly, with standard capitalisation — for example "Software Development", "Hospitality", "Legal Services", "Staffing and Recruiting", "Wellness and Fitness Services". Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `linkedin_industry: ["Software Development", "IT Services and IT Consulting"]` returns records matching either.

country.description: Exact country name filter on the company's location. Use the full English country name. Note that company location is derived from where the company's team is based: this is accurate for the small companies that dominate the index, but large multinationals are attributed to a single one of their offices — combine it with other filters rather than relying on location alone when targeting global companies. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `country: ["United States", "Canada"]` returns records matching either.

state.description: Exact state or region name filter on the company's location. Accepts the full name with standard capitalisation or its abbreviation — "Texas" and "TX" both work. Canadian provinces match by their two-letter code too — "Ontario" or "ON", "British Columbia" or "BC", "Quebec" or "QC". Combine with `country` for precision. Location is team-derived in the same way as `country`, so it is most accurate for smaller companies. Accepts a single value or a list — a list matches any of its values (OR), so `state: ["Texas", "Florida"]` returns records matching either.

exclude_domain.description: Company domains to exclude. Any company on this list is dropped from the results — this is the suppression list, so pass the accounts you already have (existing customers, current vendors, your own company) and they never come back. Full URLs are normalised automatically, exactly as with `domain`. Excluded records cost you nothing: they consume no tokens and no fair use records, so excluding here is always cheaper than filtering the results yourself.

exclude_industry.description: Industries to exclude. Companies in any listed industry are dropped. Accepts the same values as `industry`. Exclusion only removes companies that positively carry one of these values, so companies with no industry on record still appear in your results.

exclude_employee_range.description: Employee count bands to exclude. Companies in any listed band are dropped. Accepts the same values as `employee_range` — for example ["1-10", "11-20"] to skip the very smallest companies, or ["5001+"] to skip enterprises.

exclude_revenue_range.description: Revenue bands to exclude. Companies in any listed band are dropped. Accepts the same values as `revenue_range` — for example ["Below $500k"] to skip the smallest companies, or ["Above $50M"] to skip large enterprises.

limit.description: Number of results to return (default: 10, max: 25).

offset.description: Number of results to skip for pagination (default: 0). Use with limit to page through results — e.g. offset: 10 to get the second page of 10 results.

post.description: The LinkedIn Profile Search API finds a person or company's LinkedIn profile from a name and company domain. Pass a full name (MoltSets splits it into first and last name for you) or send `first_name` and `last_name` separately, then add the company as a domain, for example `acme.com`. URLs are normalised automatically, so there's no need to clean up your inputs first. Run a free count first with `count_only: true` to see how many matches exist, then tighten or loosen your search before spending tokens. Full results are only charged when a match is actually found, so an empty search costs nothing. **Use this endpoint to:** - Confirm you have the right LinkedIn profile before enriching a contact - Check match volume before running a bulk search - Attach LinkedIn URLs to contact records that are missing one **Fair Use Policy:** This API is subject to our Fair Use Policy for Search. **Outcomes:** A lookup that finds nothing is not an error. It returns HTTP `200` with `status: "not_found"`, empty or null `results`, and the usual `metadata` — and costs no tokens, though it still counts as one request against your Fair Use requests limit. Read `status`, not the HTTP code, to tell a hit from a miss. The API's only `404` is an unknown or retired tool name.

name.description: Full name (e.g. 'John Smith') — parsed into first and last name automatically.

first_name.description: First name (used if `name` is not provided).

last_name.description: Last name (used if `name` is not provided).

company.description: Company domain (e.g. 'acme.com') or URL (e.g. 'https://acme.com') — normalized to domain.

company_domain.description: Alias for `company` — company domain or URL.

count_only.description: Free — returns the count of matching results without fetching data or charging tokens. Use this first to gauge result volume before committing to a full search.

post.description: The Business Email Finder API finds a person's valid work email address from just their name and company domain. It runs a LinkedIn profile search and an email lookup in a single call, and returns the email address along with the matched LinkedIn profile URL. Pass a full name or separate `first_name` and `last_name` fields, and provide the company as a domain, for example `acme.com`. URLs are normalised automatically, and tokens are only charged when an email is found. **Use this endpoint to:** - Find a prospect's work email before outreach - Fill in missing email fields on a lead list - Enrich CRM records with verified contact emails **Fair Use Policy:** This API is subject to our Fair Use Policy for Search. **Outcomes:** A lookup that finds nothing is not an error. It returns HTTP `200` with `status: "not_found"`, empty or null `results`, and the usual `metadata` — and costs no tokens, though it still counts as one request against your Fair Use requests limit. Read `status`, not the HTTP code, to tell a hit from a miss. The API's only `404` is an unknown or retired tool name.

post.description: The Business Profile Finder API finds anyone's full business profile from just their name and company domain. It runs a LinkedIn profile search and a firmographic lookup in a single call, and returns the person's full business profile: name, job title, seniority, LinkedIn summary, skills, location, business email, hashed business emails, and personal emails, plus company firmographics such as industry, NAICS and SIC codes, headcount, and revenue. Pass `include_experience: true` to add the person's full job history. Pass a full name or separate `first_name` and `last_name` fields, and provide the company as a domain, for example `acme.com`. URLs are normalised automatically, and tokens are only charged when a match is found. **Use this endpoint to:** - Build a complete picture of a contact and their employer in one call - Qualify leads with company context before outreach - Enrich CRM records with job title and firmographic data **Fair Use Policy:** This API is subject to our Fair Use Policy for Search. **Response fields:** - `summary` is the person's LinkedIn "about" text. `position_summary` describes their current role. - `skills` and `interests` are arrays of strings. `connection_count` is the person's LinkedIn connection count, capped at `500`. Like LinkedIn's own "500+", a value of `500` means 500 or more. - `business_email_md5s` holds the MD5 of every business email MoltSets holds for the person. `business_email_sha256s` holds the SHA256 of the same emails. It is an array of roles, each with `title`, `company`, `company_linkedin_url`, `start_date`, `end_date`, `is_current`, `seniority`, `function`, and `description`. More than one role can be current. A current role has no `end_date`. Any field without data is left out of a role. - In a found profile, a field with no data can be left out of `results` (or `company`) rather than returned as `null` or `[]`. This applies to fields such as `skills`, `interests`, `current_role_start_date`, `sic_codes`, and `revenue`. risk_score.description: Send-safety grade for the mailbox — deliverability, NOT whether the address belongs to the person looked up. Read `status`, not the HTTP code, to tell a hit from a miss. The API's only `404` is an unknown or retired tool name.

The Get Account API retrieves your MoltSets account details: account name, current plan, account status, remaining credit balance, whether personal-email lookups are on your plan (`personal_email_available`), live Fair Use standing (`fair_use`), phone token balance and phone token subscription, number of API keys, and user count.

**Use this endpoint to:**
- Check account health programmatically
- Verify your account is active
- Check whether `linkedin_to_personal_email_usa` and `linkedin_to_best_personal_email_usa` are available on your plan
- Check your phone token balance before running `linkedin_to_mobile_phone`
- Display account information inside your own application or dashboard
